207: After a trip through the cytoplasm (Sm ring loading, cap trimethylation), snRNPs re-enter the nucleus and stop here. U4 and U6 are paired with the help of SART3, then joined by U5: the U4/U6·U5 tri-snRNP is ready for the spliceosome. After each splicing event, the separated U4, U5 and U6 come back to be reassembled; the high local concentration speeds up this step.
209: “Gemini of Cajal bodies”: a twin body, most often merged with the Cajal body. In the cytoplasm the SMN complex (SMN and Gemin2 to 8) loads the ring of seven Sm proteins around each snRNA, then escorts the snRNP on its way back. Loss of both copies of SMN1 (5q13): spinal muscular atrophy. The SMN2 copy, whose exon 7 is mostly skipped, compensates only in part; nusinersen and risdiplam correct this splicing.
210: Client proteins of the PML body
211: SP100, DAXX and ATRX (histone H3.3 deposition), SUMO, the ubiquitin ligase RNF4 which recognises SUMO chains and sends proteins to the proteasome, p53 and the enzymes that modify it (CBP, HIPK2). In cells that lengthen their telomeres by recombination, without telomerase (ALT), PML bodies enclose the telomeres.
212: A body of about 0.3 µm built on an RNA: NEAT1_2 (≈ 23 kb), with the proteins NONO, SFPQ and PSPC1 (DBHS family), FUS and a few dozen others. Always next to a speckle, hence its name. It retains in the nucleus RNAs carrying long edited double-stranded regions (adenosine → inosine) and sequesters proteins, especially under stress. It depends on ongoing NEAT1 transcription. Very clear in cultured cells; in tissues, only in certain cell types or under stress: it is shown here for illustration.
214: A long non-coding RNA transcribed by polymerase II, without a poly(A) tail (3′ end protected by a triple helix, like MALAT1). In the paraspeckle each molecule is folded into a hairpin: both ends at the surface, its middle at the centre, with NONO and SFPQ (green beads) — a core-shell organisation.
216: Sits on the replication-dependent histone genes: the large cluster at 6p22 (about fifty genes) and the one at 1q21. It concentrates NPAT, FLASH and the U7 snRNP. In S phase, cyclin E–CDK2 phosphorylates NPAT and transcription surges. Histone pre-mRNA has neither introns nor a poly(A) tail: it is cut after a stem-loop recognised by SLBP, at the position specified by U7. The erythroblast, which is still dividing, must double its histone stock at every cycle.
218: Three nested phases. Fibrillar centre (FC, pale sphere): reserve of the transcription machinery. Dense fibrillar component (DFC, green): first retouching of the pre-rRNA. Granular component (GC, everything else): subunit assembly. Pre-rRNA is born at the FC/DFC border and matures as it moves away: a radial flow, from centre to surface. A human nucleolus has several dozen FC/DFC units, each with 2 or 3 active genes; about ten are drawn here.
220: Reserve of the machinery: RNA polymerase I (purple), UBF, the SL1 factor, treacle protein (pale yellow). It contains the ribosomal DNA; active genes lie at its surface, at the border with the DFC. Mutations in TCOF1 (treacle), POLR1C or POLR1D: Treacher Collins syndrome, through a shortage of ribosomes in neural crest cells.
222: A repeat unit of about 43 kb: 13.3 kb transcribed, then an intergenic spacer of about 30 kb carrying promoter, enhancers and terminators. The promoter (yellow bead) is recognised by UBF and SL1 (TBP and its polymerase I-specific TAFs), which recruit the polymerase through RRN3. At the end of the gene (red bead), the protein TTF-1 bound to the terminators stops the polymerase. Active copies have lost their regular nucleosomes and are covered with UBF; silent copies are methylated and compact. Stretched out, the gene would measure 4.5 µm: it is drawn coiled on the surface of the fibrillar centre.
224: Thirteen subunits, a single product: the 47S pre-rRNA. About a hundred polymerases follow one another on each active gene, one every 130 bp or so — the “Christmas tree” of Miller spreads. Speed ≈ 95 nucleotides per second: the gene is traversed in 2 min 20 s (real speed here). Ribosomal RNA makes up about 80 % of a cell's RNA. Insensitive to α-amanitin; blocked by low-dose actinomycin D.
226: Each polymerase trails its transcript, the longer the further it has travelled. As soon as it emerges, the 5′ end is grasped by fibrillarin, which pulls it towards the DFC, and by the U3 snoRNP. The 5′ETS–18S region folds with about 70 factors into the SSU processome, a 4.5 MDa particle (blue-green bead at the tip of the transcript), the precursor of the small subunit. Order of regions in the 47S: 5′ETS – 18S – ITS1 – 5.8S – ITS2 – 28S – 3′ETS. Nearly half will be discarded.
228: Fibrillarin is the methyltransferase of C/D snoRNPs, with NOP56, NOP58 and SNU13. The small guide RNA pairs with the rRNA and designates the nucleotide whose ribose will be 2′-O-methylated (donor: SAM): just over 100 sites on human rRNAs. Its glycine- and arginine-rich domain makes it condense into 18 to 24 clusters around each fibrillar centre: these form the DFC and steer the pre-rRNA outwards. The U3 snoRNP is a special C/D: it does not methylate, it guides the first cleavages.
230: Dyskerin (DKC1), NOP10, NHP2 and GAR1 around a double-hairpin guide RNA. Dyskerin converts the designated uridine into pseudouridine (Ψ): about a hundred sites on human rRNAs. The same protein stabilises telomerase RNA, which carries an H/ACA domain: its mutations cause X-linked dyskeratosis congenita (short telomeres, bone marrow failure).
232: A sub-phase described in 2023 at the outer edge of the DFC. There the protein URB1 (orange) holds the 3′ end of the pre-rRNA while the U8 snoRNA recognises it and the 3′ETS is removed. Without URB1, miscut intermediates are destroyed by the exosome and 28S production drops.
234: Precursor of the large subunit, assembled in the granular component: 28S and 5.8S rRNAs still joined by ITS2, 5S rRNA, RPL proteins and dozens of assembly factors (GTPases, helicases, AAA+ ATPases such as midasin). ITS2 is cut then trimmed by the exosome. The particle leaves the nucleolus, finishes maturing in the nucleoplasm and exits through a pore with the exportin CRM1 and its adaptor NMD3; final touches in the cytoplasm. Paler shade towards the surface: more mature particles.
236: Precursor of the small subunit: after the cleavages in the 5′ETS and ITS1, the SSU processome comes apart and releases a particle carrying an 18S rRNA still extended at its 3′ end, and the RPS proteins. It crosses the granular component quickly and leaves the nucleus through a pore (CRM1); in the cytoplasm the endonuclease NOB1 makes the last cut. Diamond-Blackfan anaemia: one ribosomal protein is at half dose (RPS19 in a quarter of cases); nucleolar stress stabilises p53 and blocks erythroblasts first.
238: The most abundant protein of the granular component. A pentamer (pink ring) whose acidic regions bind the arginine-rich motifs of nucleolar proteins, and whose C-terminal domain binds rRNA: these multiple weak bonds make the liquid phase of the GC. A maturing particle offers fewer and fewer handholds and eventually leaves the nucleolus. NPM1 is mutated in about a third of adult acute myeloid leukaemias: the mutant protein moves to the cytoplasm.
240: The fourth rRNA, 5S (121 nucleotides), is the only one transcribed outside the nucleolus: by RNA polymerase III, from repeated genes at 1q42. It arrives bound to the proteins RPL5 and RPL11 and will form the central protuberance of the large subunit. When ribosome production is disturbed, this free 5S RNP binds MDM2, which stabilises p53: this is the nucleolar stress signal.
